paragraphs.heading: Mirror-image molecules
paragraphs.text: An enantiomer, also called an optical isomer or optical antipode, is one of a pair of molecules that are mirror images of each other but cannot be superposed, meaning laid one on the other so they match. Your hands are the classic picture: you cannot fit a left hand onto a right hand without first turning it into its mirror image. No amount of turning the whole molecule around, or changing its shape by flexing, converts one enantiomer into the other. The difference lies purely in chirality and in fixed three-dimensional relationships.

paragraphs.heading: Where they fit
paragraphs.text: Stereoisomers include both enantiomers and diastereomers. Diastereomers also share a molecular formula and cannot be superposed on each other, but they are not mirror images. In an enantiomer, the asymmetric atom is called a chirality center, also known as a chiral center or asymmetric center. A compound with exactly one asymmetric atom, or any odd number, is always chiral. With an even number, the atoms can be arranged in mirror-symmetric pairs so the compound lacks chirality; these are meso compounds, such as meso tartaric acid with its two asymmetric carbons.

paragraphs.heading: Turning light
paragraphs.text: Chiral structures rotate plane-polarized light. A dextrorotatory molecule, marked (+), turns the plane clockwise, and a levorotatory one, marked (−), turns it counterclockwise. A racemic mixture, also called a racemate, holds equal amounts of both enantiomers and does not rotate light. In nature most chiral compounds occur as only one enantiomer: proteins, for example, take in only the L form of the amino acid alanine.

paragraphs.heading: Three ways to name them
paragraphs.text: Chemists have three common ways to say which enantiomer they mean. The R/S system follows the molecule's geometry around a chiral center, using the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog priority rules, which give the highest priority to the group or atom with the largest atomic number. The (+)/(−) system, once written with d- and l-, follows optical rotation, and the D/L system relates the molecule to the enantiomers of glyceraldehyde. The letters trace back to Latin: laevus and sinister mean left, while dexter means right, as does rectus in the sense of correct.

paragraphs.heading: One form or both in a drug
paragraphs.text: An enantiopure compound contains only one of the two enantiomers, and such compositions give better therapeutic effect. The antidepressant citalopram is a racemate, a 1:1 mixture of its (S) and (R) forms, while escitalopram is the pure (S) form. Typical doses of escitalopram are about half those of citalopram. Swapping a racemic drug for an enantiopure one is called a chiral switch.

paragraphs.heading: Twins with different jobs
paragraphs.text: In many cases the two enantiomers have distinct effects. Eli Lilly sold the two forms of propoxyphene separately: dextropropoxyphene as an analgesic called Darvon, and levopropoxyphene as an antitussive called Novrad. Even the two trade names mirror each other. The herbicide mecoprop is a racemic mixture, but the weed-killing activity belongs to its (R)-(+) enantiomer.
